paragraphs.source_en: Sultanic Savionhs 161 Rabbi Elijah ben Elkanah Capsali of Candia (Irdklion, on Venetian Crete), wrote ecstatically of Mehmed II, Bayezid II, Selim I, and Suleiman I. He saw them as redeemers of the Jews, players in the cosmic drama between the forces of good and evil that preceded the advent of the messiah.? While Greeks lamented how ‘all things turned to evil. What and how and why? Because of our sins!’, non-Greek Jews had the opposite reaction to the fall of Constantinople and the Byzantine Empire.‘ The sultans were ‘messengers of God’ who punished ‘wicked’ nations and gathered the exiled Jews.° Capsali claimed that God had promised Osman, the founder of the Ottoman Empire, ‘a kingdom as hard as iron’.

paragraphs.source_en: Jews looked to Suleiman I with hope, for he was the tenth Ottoman sultan, and, as the Torah predicts, ‘every tenth one shall be holy to God’ and ‘in his days Judah shall be delivered and Israel shall dwell secure’ and ‘a redeemer shall come to Zion’."° Imbued with such millenarian expectations, Solomon Molho— the former Diego Pires, a Portuguese converso who had returned to Judaism in the Ottoman Empire, where he studied Kabbalah (Jewish mysticism)—proclaimed himself as the messiah around 1525. In Regensburg, Bavaria, he.had an audience with Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. The meeting did not go well, and Molho was turned over to the Inquisition.
